line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Be2 O-O Bg5 Nbd7 h4 h6 Be3 e5 d5 b6 Qd2 Kh7 g4 Nc5 f3 a5 Nh3 Rh8 g5
teaches: In a locked centre the pawn storm is the argument, and its best moves hit two things at once — a pawn advance that attacks a piece and a pawn together forces a concession whichever way it is answered, and every trade it causes opens another line toward the king.
explains: The pawn steps to g5 and attacks the knight on f6 and the pawn on h6 in the same move. One of them must give: the knight retreats or the pawns trade, and either answer opens lines on the side of the board where all the storming pawns already point.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Be2 O-O Bg5 Nbd7 h4 h6 Be3 e5 d5 b6 Qd2 Kh7 g4 Nc5 f3 a5 Nh3 Rh8 g5 Ng8 h5 Bxh3 Rxh3 gxh5 O-O-O
teaches: In a tense position with many captures available, two disciplines pay together: let the opponent be the one who takes — you only recapture, keeping every file that opens working for you — and ask which of your pieces is missing in action. The move that signs in the last absent piece usually outranks every capture on the board.
explains: Castling long brings the rook from a1 — the one piece that had no job — into the game while the king steps to safety, and the kingside tension stays exactly as it was: unresolved, on the opponent's clock. Whoever takes first there opens lines for the side that was ready.
structural: the last absent piece signed in before any capture — tension held so the opener pays for the opening
